summary.summary: Covering report inviting Newport's Governance and Audit Committee to review and feed back on the draft Annual Governance Statement (AGS) 2025/26 before it is approved and published. The AGS self-assessment, run against the seven principles of the CIPFA/SOLACE 'Delivering Good Governance in Local Government' framework, has identified 25 areas of improvement for action in 2026/27. This cover sheet contains no financial figures and no language suggesting financial or governance distress; the substantive AGS assessment itself is a separate attachment not included in this cached PDF.

findings.headline: Confirmed pay award of 3.3% exceeds budget assumption 3.0%, creating recurring pressure with no mitigation identified
findings.detail: Budget was set assuming 3.0% pay award. Actual confirmed award is 3.3% (0.3% higher). Report notes: 'Current forecasts reflect the 3.3% pay award and, unless offset by additional Welsh Government funding, the increased pay costs will place ongoing pressure on the Council's financial position.' This is an employee cost base of £295m+ at risk.
findings.matters: Permanent recurring gap on largest cost base (employee costs); no service mitigation identified; requires either additional funding or service reduction
findings.figures: 3.3% actual award vs 3.0% budgeted (0.3 percentage point shortfall on employee base of ~£298m forecast spend = ~£900k recurring gap)
findings.quote: The approved 2026/27 revenue budget was based on an assumed NJC pay award of 3.0%. The confirmed pay award of 3.3% is therefore higher than the budgeted provision and creates a recurring budget pressure for the Council. Current forecasts reflect the 3.3% pay award and, unless offset by additional Welsh Government funding, the increased pay costs will place ongoing pressure on the Council's financial position.

findings.headline: Adult social care supported living demand 202 service users against budget 189; overspend £1.072m driven by volume exceeding assumptions
findings.detail: Supported Living has 202 service users against budgeted 189 (13 above forecast). Average cost £1,979 per week remains below budget of £2,011 per user, but volume excess drives £1.072m overspend. Described as continuation of demand pressures seen in 2025/26 despite mitigation actions.
findings.matters: Indicates unbudgeted service user growth continuing despite cost controls, suggesting demand prediction is unreliable and social care spending will continue to exceed forecasts
findings.figures: 202 service users vs budget 189 (13 over), overspend £1.072m, average cost £1,979 vs budget £2,011 per week
findings.quote: The principal driver of the overspend is continued demand growth within Supported Living, where expenditure is forecast to exceed budget by £1.072m. Although the average cost per service user of £1,979 remains below the budgeted assumption of £2,011, the service is currently supporting 202 individuals compared with a budgeted provision for 189, resulting in a significant full-year pressure.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance only £7.5m, representing just 2.5% of net budget excluding schools; total reserves mostly earmarked with only £26.2m unallocated
findings.detail: Of £119.6m total reserves, £37.1m is committed to PFI, £13.0m is schools' own reserves, £28.8m capital-related, £7m risk management, leaving only £26.2m discretionary. General reserve of £7.5m is described as 'low' and 'should only be accessed where absolutely necessary.' HoF recommended increasing this at budget-setting.
findings.matters: Council lacks sufficient unallocated reserves to absorb significant adverse variance; any major service pressure or missed grant will force drawdown of earmarked reserves and de-prioritise planned initiatives
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £7.5m (2.5% of net budget ex-schools), total reserves £119.6m, earmarked commitments £37.1m (PFI) + £13m (schools) + £28.8m (capital) + £7m (risk) = £85.9m, discretionary £26.2m
findings.quote: The general level of cover provided by this balance is low, standing at 2.5% of the net budget, excluding schools. This reinforces the fact that this should only be accessed where absolutely necessary and should continue to be increased at the earliest opportunity as the HoF recommended to the Council when setting the current year's budget.

findings.headline: Balanced position depends entirely on £1.985m capital financing underspend explicitly described as unsustainable; service area overspends are actually £4.193m
findings.detail: Reported £0.408m net overspend masks £4.193m underlying service area overspends, offset only by £1.636m contingency use and £1.985m capital financing underspend (lower MRP and interest payable due to capital slippage). Report explicitly warns: 'this mitigation is not sustainable and cannot be relied upon in future years, as the underspend is largely attributable to the timing of capital expenditure. As the capital programme is delivered, the capital financing budget will be fully utilised.'
findings.matters: Headline balance is illusory; underlying deficit of £4.2m is being masked by non-recurrence, creating false confidence in financial position and hiding deterioration for 2027/28
findings.figures: £4.193m service overspends, £1.985m capital financing underspend, £1.636m contingency, net reported £0.408m overspend
findings.quote: Temporary financial mitigation is available through a forecast underspend within the capital financing budget, estimated at £1.9m. This provides some short-term flexibility in managing emerging revenue pressures during 2026/27. However, this mitigation is not sustainable and cannot be relied upon in future years, as the underspend is largely attributable to the timing of capital expenditure. As the capital programme is delivered, the capital financing budget will be fully utilised, and this resource will no longer be available to offset revenue pressures.

findings.headline: 49 of 56 schools forecasting in-year overspend; school reserves falling £3.584m from £13.054m to £9.469m with 59% of overspend recurring
findings.detail: School reserves forecast to fall by £3.584m in one year. One school already in deficit position; several with dangerously low forecast reserves. Analysis shows 59% of the in-year overspend is recurring expenditure, not one-off costs, meaning schools face structural budget gaps. Report warns: 'For some schools, this is an unsustainable position.'
findings.matters: Schools are consuming reserves at an unsustainable rate with recurring overspends, creating high risk of mass deficit positions and intervention within 1–2 years
findings.figures: 49 of 56 schools overspending, reserves fall £3.584m in year, 59% of overspend recurring, 1 school currently in deficit, opening reserves £13.054m, closing forecast £9.469m
findings.quote: 49 out of 56 schools are forecasting an in-year overspend on their revenue funding…the latest monitoring position shows that several schools are forecasting relatively low reserve balances for March 2026, and 1 school is forecasting a deficit position…An analysis of the forecast overspend has identified that approx. 59% is to fund recurring expenditure. For some schools, this is an unsustainable position, as surplus balances are limited, and, therefore, there is a risk of entering a deficit position in future years.
